query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The native oxide film already present on as-received Q235 steel can be thermally tuned via controlled annealing to develop a denser, more uniform passivation layer that slows chloride-induced corrosion at both room temperature and 700–900 °C, while overly high or inadequate annealing fails to produce these beneficial structural modifications.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel having a native, irregular oxide film formed under ambient conditions.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the annealing treatment (e.g., different temperatures and durations) on Q235 steel, with one set left untreated as a reference and another optionally coated with an HEA to compare effects.
generation.conditions: Exposure to aggressive chloride-rich salt environments at room temperature and high temperature (700–900 °C) during corrosion testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural evolution and compositional homogenization of the passive oxide film on Q235 steel, including changes in film density, grain boundary structure, and phase composition.
generation.mechanism: Controlled annealing modifies the native oxide layer by promoting beneficial phase transformations and densification. At an optimum annealing condition, the oxide film becomes continuous and less porous, impeding chloride penetration. In contrast, insufficient or excessive annealing results in films with microstructural defects (e.g., cracks or nonuniform phases) that provide preferential sites for pitting and corrosion- related degradation, especially under high-temperature salt exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Q235 steel annealed at optimal conditions will exhibit significantly reduced mass change, lower pitting density, and improved film integrity compared to untreated samples. At both room temperature and 700–900 °C, these improvements should be measurable via surface characterization (e.g., XPS, SEM) and performance metrics, whereas suboptimal treatments yield little to no protection improvement.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel, which has a native oxide film with irregular coverage and moderate resistance to salt-induced corrosion.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies predominantly to Q235 steel in its as-received state under aggressive chloride salt conditions. It may not hold in non-corrosive or controlled inert environments, or when additional protective coatings (beyond the studied HEA option) are present.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal annealing temperature and duration for achieving the best passivation properties remain uncertain, as does the quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance across the temperature regimes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of as-received Q235 steel samples. Subject each set to different annealing treatments (e.g., no treatment, moderate annealing at an intermediate temperature, and high annealing temperatures) while keeping all other variables constant. Expose all samples to an identical aggressive chloride salt environment at both room temperature and at ~800 °C. A parallel test group can include a HEA-coated variant for additional reference. After exposure, evaluate corrosion damage through mass change measurements, pitting counts, and detailed surface analyses via SEM and XPS.
measurements: XPS analysis of oxide film composition and uniformity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If controlled annealing does not lead to any statistically significant improvement in passivation film integrity or reduction in corrosion indicators compared to untreated Q235 steel across both temperature regimes, the hypothesis that controlled thermal treatment is the governing cause for improved corrosion protection is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

cited_evidence.text: The use of HEAs in nuclear applications depends greatly on their microstructural stability in the extreme environments of the operating conditions. Although Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 alloy shows good mechanical properties and relatively high resistance to radiation damage, this study showed that the alloy experienced phase instability at 700 °C after 1000 hours. Cr-rich particles were found to precipitate in the alloy, even well beneath the corrosion affected region, after the high temperature exposure during the corrosion test. Just underneath the surface, few fine circular Cr-rich precipitates were observed. As the distance from the surface increased, the Cr-rich precipitates’ concentration increased and their morphology became more needle-shaped as shown in Fig. 6. Then, the precipitates’ concentration decreased significantly but persisted through the entire thickness of the sample as shown in Figs. 6 and 9. These changes in the concentration and morphology of the Cr-rich precipitates indicate that the precipitation process not only depends on both the annealing temperature and duration, but also on the Mn concentration in the alloy, which varies due to its dissolution in the salt.

TiAlN and ZrN films have been widely used as protective coating. The NbTiAlSi system HEA films have been reported to possess high hardness and modulus [,,]. CoCrFeNiAl0.3 films fabricated by RF sputtering demonstrate better corrosion resistance than in 3.5 wt. % NaCl solution. The hardness of CoCrFeNiAl0.3 can reach 11.5 GPa. Moreover, the addition of non-metallic elements has been shown to be an effective means for improving the properties of HEAs []. In this regard, we prepared a new five primary element NbTiAlSiZr HEA of equimolar content, and then used the processing methods and RN conditions—which were different from those previously reported in [], using the radio frequency (RF) magnetron sputtering equipment, processes, and other parameters of fixed technologies—to prepare the NbTiAlSiZrNx HEA thin films under different RN values (0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50%) and gases (i.e., RN is the only process variable). Then the roughness, color, and performance of these thin films were studied. frame.system: Q235 steel in its as-received (pre-exposure) state, with consideration for incorporating high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings or related annealing treatments.
frame.goal: To develop a testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains the corrosion degradation or retention of protection in Q235 steel under both room temperature and high-temperature (700–900 °C) regimes, particularly under aggressive salt exposure.
frame.limitation: Previous studies largely focused on performance metrics (hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability) and did not elucidate the underlying mechanisms by which corrosion protection persists or fails across different temperature regimes. Additionally, integrated studies that combine HEA treatments, annealing, and hot-corrosion assessments are minimal.
root_cause_cues: why corrosion protection persists or fails
combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal
constraints: The hypothesis must be testable in a controlled study
It should isolate the key causative factor(s) (e.g., microstructural changes, passivation film formation/degradation)
The study must compare Q235 steel with an appropriate reference (e.g., untreated vs. HEA-coated or annealed variants)
Observations should be predicted relative to established benchmarks from earlier studies

It must specify conditions under which the hypothesis applies (aggressive salt environment at both room and high temperature) and conditions where it should not (e.g., absence of annealing effects or non-corrosive environments)
The design should include an observation whose occurrence would falsify the hypothesis
regime: Controlled annealing conditions for microstructural evolution
prior_attempts: Studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels focused on performance improvements (hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, mass change) without establishing the underlying corrosion mechanism across different temperatures
Limited investigations combining HEA deposition, annealing processes, and hot-corrosion performance assessment, leading to a gap in understanding the governing processes

families.principle: Integrating experimental controlled studies with simulation-based insights to correlate observed passivation behavior with underlying atomic-scale mechanisms.

families.best_lever: Combine controlled annealing and corrosion experiments on Q235 steel (with and without HEA coatings) with simulations that predict microstructural evolution and passivation kinetics, using simulation outputs to guide and interpret experimental observations and pinpoint the key transitions that indicate failure or sustainability of the protective layer.

families.principle: Modeling atomic diffusion, phase transformations, and interface reactions that govern passivation layer stability and microstructural evolution during annealing and salt exposure.

cues_against: the question emphasizes a testable controlled experiment, and simulation alone may not provide directly verifiable predictions without experimental validation
families.best_lever: Develop molecular dynamics or phase-field simulations that model the diffusion of corrosive species and oxidation kinetics at both ambient and high temperatures, generating predictions on passivation layer stability for experimental comparison.
